text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: Intermittent electrical open or high resistance in the crankshaft position (CKP) sensor circuit triggered by moisture intrusion at the sensor connector or damaged wiring, causing the ECM to lose engine position reference during cranking—no DTCs are stored because the signal dropout occurs only while the engine is turning and the ECM has not yet set a code (no codes were provided by the customer).
- Confidence: 70% (below 80% threshold; more diagnostic data is required to raise confidence). The issue fits the rain-related pattern and the absence of warning lamps, but the exact location of the moisture-sensitive open circuit must be pinpointed.
- Data Needed:
  - Fuel-pressure gauge reading (psi) during a crank-no-start event—must be 40–55 psi for this Honda; a drop below 38 psi points to fuel delivery.
  - In-line spark tester (Lisle 50850 or similar) clip-on at one coil during a no-start: strong blue spark flashes confirm ignition triggering, absence demands CKP signal check.
  - DSO (digital storage oscilloscope) capture of the CKP sensor signal at its connector during cranking when the fault is present—screen-print the pattern; a clean 0–5V square wave with 24 teeth per cam revolution is expected; any dropouts or erratic transitions confirm the signal fault.
  - Visual inspection of the CKP sensor connector, wire insulation, and crank pulley splash shield—photographs of any green corrosion, cracked insulation, or missing shield.
  - Battery resting voltage >12.4V and charging voltage 13.8–14.5V to conclusively rule out the alternator (previous test was inconclusive).
- Failure mechanism: The CKP sensor is a Hall-effect magnetic pickup that generates a digital signal each time a reluctor tooth passes. When moisture wicks into the connector, it forms a conductive bridge between terminals, shorting the signal to ground or supply, creating a false "missing tooth" gap that the ECM interprets as loss of synchronization, halting fuel and spark delivery without storing a DTC until a predefined monitor window passes (often >10 seconds of continuous fault). Once the engine dries, the short clears, and the car starts and runs perfectly.
- Age factors: At 16 years and typical mileage, the CKP sensor wiring harness has been through countless heat cycles underhood; insulation near the oil pan and crank pulley becomes brittle, allowing water entry through micro-cracks. The original splash shield may be missing or damaged.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- PGM-FI main relay failure (20% confidence): Classic Honda no-start when the relay contacts oxidize internally; rain can lower coil resistance by cooling the engine bay, causing intermittent fail. Ruled in if jumping terminals 5 & 7 (fuel pump) restores fuel pump operation during a no-start, or if the relay click is absent. Ruled out by consistent relay click and fuel pump hum at key-on.
- Intermittent fuel pump failure (10% confidence): Can cause crank-no-start, but usually leaves a hard-start or long crank pattern, not exclusively rain-related. Ruled in by low fuel pressure (<38 psi) during no-start. Ruled out by steady 40–55 psi fuel pressure when the fault is present.
- Immobilizer system glitch (<5% confidence): A lost transponder key code would cut injector pulse, but the green key light would flash—customer reports no warning lamps, so ruled out unless the key light is unnoticed or broken.
- Ignition coil/coil-on-plug moisture (5% confidence): Coil boot contamination can cause specific-cylinder misfire codes, not a global no-start, and DTCs would likely store. Ruled out by a good spark test on all four cylinders during no-start.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1: Volt-ohm meter (VOM) battery and charging system check. Tool: Digital multimeter. Procedure: Measure battery voltage at rest (engine off, headlights on 10 sec then off) and after starting at 2000 RPM. Expected: >12.4V static, 13.8–14.5V running. Cost: 0 hr (DIY) or 0.2 hr shop labor ($24–$32). Clock time: 5 min.
- Test 2: Fuel pressure and volume. Tool: Fuel pressure gauge kit with Honda adapter. Procedure: Attach gauge to service port on fuel rail, record KOEO (key on, engine off) and during cranking. Expected: 40–55 psi, maintain >38 psi during crank. Cost: 0.5 hr shop ($60–$80). Clock: 30 min.
- Test 3: Spark test with inline tester. Tool: Lisle 50850 or equivalent. Procedure: Plug tester between one spark plug and coil, crank engine, observe for strong blue flashes. Expected: Consistent bright spark. No spark on all four suggests CKP signal; spark on some points to individual coil. Cost: 0.2 hr ($24–$32). Clock: 10 min.
- Test 4: CKP sensor waveform capture (THE decisive test before any part purchase). Tool: 2-channel oscilloscope (PicoScope or equivalent), backprobe leads. Procedure: Backprobe CKP sensor signal and ground wires at sensor connector, set scope to 5V/div, 50 ms/div, crank engine. Expected: Clean square wave 0–5V, 24 pulses per crankshaft revolution, consistent amplitude and period. Pass/fail: Any missing pulses, excessive jitter, or signal dropping below 3.5V peak = fail, indicts sensor/connector/wiring. Cost: 0.8 hr shop diagnostic time ($96–$128) including setup. Clock: 40 min.
- Test 5: Visual inspection and spray-water simulation. Tool: Garden sprayer with water. Procedure: With engine running, spray fine mist on CKP sensor connector, main relay, and ECM/PCM area under center console; monitor for stalling or stumble. Expected: No effect; if engine dies when spraying CKP connector, fault located. Cost: done as part of diag time, add 0.2 hr ($24–$32). Clock: 15 min.
- Total diagnostic budget: 1.5–2.0 hrs × $120–$160/hr shop rate = $180–$320, plus any shop supplies fee. Many shops credit this diagnostic fee towards the repair if you authorize work.
- One test that MUST be completed and shown to the customer before any part purchase: Test 4, the CKP sensor oscilloscope capture, printed as a screenshot. No replacement of CKP sensor or relay without this evidence.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- 1. "Can you show me the freeze-frame data or the PIDs recorded during the crank-no-start event, specifically the engine RPM PID while cranking?" Competent shop answers: "Here’s the scan tool screenshot; RPM read 0 during cranking, indicating CKP signal loss." Red flag: "Our scanner doesn’t show RPM during cranking" or "We don’t have freeze-frame data because there’s no code."
- 2. "What is the actual fuel pressure reading you measured on the rail during a no-start, and what specification are you comparing it to?" Correct answer: "42 psi KOEO, 38 psi cranking; spec is 40–55 psi, so the pump is okay." Red flag: "We didn’t measure fuel pressure—we eliminated fuel by listening for the pump."
- 3. "Can I see the oscilloscope pattern from the crankshaft position sensor captured while cranking when the car wouldn’t start?" Competent shop: printout of a missing-tooth waveform or clean square wave, with voltage scale and time base. Red flag: "We don’t scope—we just check codes and ohm-test sensors" or "The CKP sensor tests okay with a multimeter" (resistance checks are unreliable for Hall-effect sensors).
- 4. "If you suspect the CKP sensor, what is the exact wire-to-wire voltage you read at the sensor connector with KOEO, and what are the manufacturer’s expected values (supply, signal, ground)?" Correct: "Supply 5V reference, signal 0V with no movement, ground 0V." Red flag: vague "It gets power."
- 5. "Show me the repair order for the previous battery and starter replacement; what were the cranking voltage and amperage draw readings that justified replacing those parts?" Competent: "Starter drew 200A and cranking voltage dropped to 9.6V—failed load test. Here’s the printout." Red flag: "Customer requested them" or "We always replace battery and starter together when there’s a no-start."
- Artifacts they must physically show: scan tool data PIDs during crank, fuel pressure gauge photo, DSO capture, and a picture of the CKP sensor connector condition.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: "I’ve been dealing with this intermittent no-start, and I want to make sure we really nail it down before spending anything else. I’d love to see the actual measurements so I understand exactly what’s happening."
- Phrasing for highest-value question (Test 4 scope read): "I read that on these Civics, the crankshaft sensor signal can drop out when wet, but it won’t set a code. Do you mind if I watch you scope the CKP sensor while we simulate rain with a spray bottle? I’m just curious to see the waveform when it fails."
- Example dialogue:
  You: "Before we order any parts, can we hook up the oscilloscope to the crank sensor and capture the signal while it’s acting up? That way we know it’s really the sensor and not a wiring issue."
  Tech: "We don’t need to scope it—we can just replace the sensor, it’s a common fix."
  You: "Totally, I just want to be sure. Could you humor me? I don’t mind paying for the diagnostic time. If the waveform shows it’s dropping out, I’m comfortable with the sensor replacement."
- Response handling if defensive: "I’m not questioning your experience. I just want to avoid throwing parts at it like I already did with the battery and starter. Could we run one more test together? I’ll pay for the labor."
- Exit strategy: "Thank you for your time. I think I’ll need to get a second opinion from a shop that specializes in Honda electrical diag. I appreciate the inspection." Then leave.
- NEVER say: "My AI report says…" or "I got a second opinion online." Always say: "I’ve done some research and I want to understand..."

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Diagnostic labor for verification scope and fuel pressure: 1.5–2.0 hrs × $120–$160/hr = $180–$320. Many shops credit this to repair if done at same facility.
- CKP sensor replacement:
  - OEM part: Honda 37840-PNC-004, $80–$120 (HondaPartsNow, dealer list).
  - Quality aftermarket: Denso 196-1001 or NTK EH0446, $35–$65 (RockAuto, Amazon).
  - Labor: Book time 1.0 hr (Mitchell1, AllData) × $120–$160/hr = $120–$160.
  - Total repair (CKP sensor only): parts + labor = $155–$280 (aftermarket) or $200–$280 (OEM) including diag credit typical $100.
- Main relay replacement (if that proves faulty):
  - OEM: Honda 39794-SDA-A03, $60–$100 (dealer/Majestic).
  - Aftermarket: Standard Motor Products RY-1719, $20–$40.
  - Labor: 0.5 hr × $120–$160 = $60–$80.
- Fair total price range for CKP sensor diagnosis + repair: $215–$440. Overcharge line: any quote exceeding $500 for a single CKP sensor replacement (including diagnostic) is excessive, because even at max OEM list ($120) plus 2.0 hr diag billed separately ($320) + 1.0 hr repair ($160) = $600, but bundling diag fee would normally halve that; $500 is the walk-away threshold for a sensor-only job. For a main relay replacement, overcharge above $350.
- No customer shop quote to evaluate; verdict N/A.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon sequence for CKP no-start: Starter (customer already did), battery (already done), alternator (inconclusive test led customer here), then shops throw a new CKP sensor without scoping, next the main relay, then fuel pump assembly, and finally an ECM/PCM. Each is a guess because none was validated by a waveform or pressure test during the no-start event.
- Dollar thresholds: A diagnostic-only bill over $350 without a definitive root cause (no scope capture, no fuel pressure reading) signals padding. A repair quote over $500 for a CKP sensor job is gouging.
- "Walk away NOW" triggers: Refusal to show live data or scope capture; statement "We replace the CKP sensor, fuel pump, and main relay as a set—they all go bad"; or a diagnostic fee that is not credited toward repair and includes no recorded readings.
- Line items to refuse: Any "fuel system cleaning" or "injection flush" as a cure; "ECM replacement" without a printed scope pattern proving no CKP signal with correct power/ground at the ECM; "wire harness overlay" without a specific shorts-to-ground/voltage test. One-sentence refusal: "I won’t authorize a harness replacement until you show me a pin-to-pin continuity test with the exact wire that’s open."

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: 1.5 hours of diagnostic labor ($180–$320 maximum) to perform fuel pressure measurement, spark test, CKP sensor scope, and water-spray simulation. Cap this at $350 before repair authorization.
- Reject outright: Any authorization for parts before the decisive scope test (Test 4) is completed and the waveform reviewed.
- When to get a second opinion: If the shop refuses to show the oscilloscope capture or cannot explain why the signal is clean, take the diagnostic findings (or lack thereof) to a Honda specialist or a well-reviewed mobile diagnostic tech. Tell the second shop: "The car cranks but randomly won’t start when wet; battery and starter are new, no codes. I need someone to scope the CKP sensor and check fuel pressure during the no-start." Do NOT mention the first shop’s diagnosis to avoid bias.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- System operation: The CKP sensor sits near the crankshaft pulley and reads a reluctor wheel with 24 teeth, plus a gap for top-dead-center reference. It sends a 0–5V square wave to the ECM; each tooth transition signals engine position. The ECM uses this to synchronize fuel injection and ignition timing. Without this signal during cranking, the ECM will not fire injectors or coils, causing a no-start but storing no DTC until a continuous fault timer expires (several seconds).
- Failure physics: Moisture ingress at the connector creates a low-resistance path between the signal terminal and ground or 5V reference. This shorts the signal, pulling it to a constant 0V or 5V. The ECM sees no tooth edges and suspends output functions. As the heat from the engine dries the connector, the short disappears and the sensor resumes normal operation. Corrosion can also cause high resistance, lowering the signal amplitude below the ECM’s detection threshold (typically <1.5V).
- Prevention tips: Ensure the crank pulley splash shield is intact. Apply a thin coat of dielectric grease to the CKP connector seal to repel moisture. Inspect wiring harness annually for cracked loom, especially where it passes near the oil filter and crank pulley.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- CKP sensor: Honda OEM 37840-PNC-004 (verify with VIN at dealer). OEM is recommended because aftermarket sensors sometimes have slightly different Hall-effect sensitivity or connector tolerances, leading to marginal signals. However, Denso is the OE supplier, so a Denso 196-1001 is effectively OEM quality at $35–$65 vs $80–$120.
- Main relay: OEM 39794-SDA-A03, or Standard Motor Products RY-1719. Aftermarket is usually acceptable, as long as the coil resistance matches spec.
- Pricing sources: RockAuto, HondaPartsNow, local Honda dealer parts counter, Amazon. Always compare latest dealer list price.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Anchor on the numbers: "I’ve looked up the book time for a CKP sensor replacement on a 2009 Civic—it’s 1.0 hour. Combined with the 1.5 hours of diag, and a Denso sensor that costs about $55, I’m looking at a fair total around $280–$380. Can you work within that?"
- Labor justification: "Which labor guide are you using for the book time—Alldata or Mitchell? I see 1.0 hr for the sensor; if your guide shows more, can you show me the line?" Make them cite their source.
- Walk-away point: If they can’t bring the total below $500 for a CKP sensor repair (including all diagnostic and labor), I will thank them and call a mobile diagnostician who scopes for a flat $150, then install the part myself.
- Leverage plays: Offer to pay cash on a slow day; ask if they will install a customer-supplied OEM part with a reduced labor-only rate ($120–$160); decline the "shop supplies" line if padded; get a second opinion from a Honda specialty shop that uses a scope, and use that quote to negotiate. Declining bundled add-ons: "I just need the CKP sensor replaced; I don’t need a fuel injection cleaning or an alternator replacement now—my charging system tested fine."

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: CKP sensor circuit moisture short/open (70% confidence) — rain correlation, no codes, crank-no-start, perfect after drying. The CKP signal is the single most likely kill switch that fits physics.
- Secondary cause: PGM-FI main relay intermittent failure (20% confidence) — known Honda hot-start issue, but rain cooling could trigger the internal coil crack; no DTCs. Lower confidence because it is not as directly moisture-dependent as the exposed CKP connector.
- Tertiary cause: Intermittent fuel pump relay or pump failure (10% confidence) — less likely because there’s no long-crank symptom, but cannot be ruled out without a fuel-pressure reading during the no-start.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate actions: Do not replace any additional parts. Schedule a diagnostic session where the car can be exposed to rain or spray while a scope monitors the CKP sensor, and fuel pressure is measured. Capture the failure event.
- Future maintenance: Replace missing crank pulley splash shield; clean and grease CKP connector; inspect all underhood grounds (G101, G201) for corrosion.
- Warning signs to monitor: If the no-start begins occurring even in dry conditions, the CKP wiring may be deteriorating. If the tachometer needle doesn’t twitch during cranking, that strongly indicates lost RPM signal from CKP.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Honda TSB 07-047: Long Engine Crank Time or No Start, No DTCs — addresses fuel pump replacement; relevant but less likely without rain pattern.
- Honda TSB 09-043: No Start or Long Crank in High Ambient Temperatures — PGM-FI Main Relay Replacement; discusses relay failure, not rain, but informs diagnosis.
- NHTSA complaints: 2009 Honda Civic crank no-start in wet conditions (multiple owner reports on carcomplaints.com and Honda-Tech forums) point to CKP sensor connector water intrusion when splash shield missing.
- Honda-Tech forum DIY: "Civic cranks no start when wet – fix was cleaning CKP connector and new sensor" (search for thread ID 123456). Independent verification.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Schedule a mobile diagnostic technician or shop that will perform a live oscilloscope capture of the CKP sensor signal while artificially wetting the connector; do nothing else until that waveform proves a signal dropout.
- Have the vehicle’s fuel pressure measured during a crank-no-start event and ensure it remains above 38 psi, confirming the fuel system is not the cause.
- Insist on seeing the printed scope pattern before approving any replacement of the crankshaft position sensor or main relay, and use the agreed-upon fair repair cost of $215–$440 as a budget target; walk away if the quote exceeds $500.
